  [image, alt text: **HumanBENCH: Learn the Rule — 6/10**

The network learns Conway’s rule successfully. The submission falls short mainly on reporting and the requested follow-up experiment.

No rubric was set beforehand for this version, so I used **2 points per prompt: complete, partial, or absent**.

| Prompt | Score | Assessment |
|---|---:|---|
| Generate labeled neighborhoods | **2/2** | All 512 unique neighborhoods, all correctly labeled. Conway’s rule is used only for labels. |
| Split and train | **2/2** | Fixed-seed shuffle, 409 training examples, 103 test examples, and a small trained network. |
| Report performance | **1/2** | Reports test accuracy and a baseline, but omits training accuracy. Error examples lack true/predicted labels. The baseline uses the full dataset rather than the test set. |
| Test symmetries | **1/2** | Checks prediction changes under three transformations, but not all rotations/reflections, and only after changing the split. |
| Improve and compare | **0/2** | Reducing training data makes an interesting harder experiment, but doesn’t supply an improvement evaluated on the same split. |

**Verification:** I ran a CPU-adapted copy because CUDA was unavailable, using three evaluator-selected PyTorch seeds. All three achieved **100% train and test accuracy on the original split**. The printed baseline was **72.66%**; always predicting dead scores **78.64% on that test set**.

With only 30% training data, test accuracy ranged from **86.63% to 96.66%**, and symmetry violations appeared. That’s a useful finding: the human deliberately made the problem harder after solving the initial version.

One methodological correction: **100% test accuracy alone doesn’t establish symmetry consistency**, because transformed test inputs may fall outside that test subset. My additional checks found no symmetry violations for the original models in these runs, but checking was still necessary.
